paragraphs: The elder had been out of his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past half-past twelve, and Dmitri, the reason they had all gathered there, still had not appeared. He seemed almost forgotten, though, and when the elder came back in, he found his guests deep in lively conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to take part too, and quite eagerly, it seemed. But he had no luck at that either. He was plainly pushed into the background, and his remarks were ignored, which only made him more irritable. He had crossed swords with Ivan before, and he could not stand a certain offhandedness Ivan showed toward him.
“Until now, at least, I have stood in the front ranks of everything progressive in Europe, and here the new generation simply ignores us,” he thought.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had given his word to sit still and keep quiet, had in fact kept quiet for some time. But he was watching his neighbor Miüsov with a mocking little smile, clearly enjoying his discomfort. He had been waiting a good while to settle old scores, and he was not going to let the chance slip. Leaning over Miüsov’s shoulder, he started teasing him again in a whisper.

“Why didn’t you leave just now, after the ‘courteously kissing’? Why did you agree to stay in such improper company? Because you felt insulted and wronged, and you stayed to prove yourself by showing off your brains. Now you won’t go until you’ve shown them what a mind you have.”
“You again?... On the contrary, I’m just leaving.”
“You’ll be the last, the last of all to go!” Fyodor Pavlovitch jabbed at him once more, almost at the very moment Father Zossima came back.

The discussion died down for a moment. The elder sat down in his old place and looked around at them all as if warmly inviting them to go on. Alyosha, who knew every expression of his face, saw that he was dreadfully tired and was forcing himself. Lately he had been prone to fainting fits from exhaustion. His face had the pallor that usually came before such attacks, and his lips were white. Yet he plainly did not want to break up the gathering. He seemed to have some purpose of his own in keeping them there. What purpose? Alyosha watched him closely.

“We were discussing this gentleman’s most interesting article,” said Father Iosif, the librarian, addressing the elder and nodding toward Ivan. “He puts forward a lot that is new, but I think the argument cuts both ways. It is an article written in reply to a book by a churchman on the question of the ecclesiastical court and how far its jurisdiction extends.”
“I’m sorry I haven’t read your article, but I’ve heard of it,” said the elder, looking keenly and intently at Ivan.
“He takes a most interesting position,” the Father Librarian went on. “As far as Church jurisdiction goes, he is apparently entirely opposed to the separation of Church and State.”
“That’s interesting. But in what sense?” Father Zossima asked Ivan.
At last Ivan answered him—not condescendingly, as Alyosha had feared, but modestly and with reserve, with obvious goodwill and, it seemed, without the slightest _arrière-pensée_.

“I start from the premise that this confusion of elements—that is, of the essential principles of Church and State—will of course go on forever, although it is impossible for them to mix, and although this confusion can lead to no consistent or even normal results, because there is falsehood at the very foundation of it. A compromise between the Church and the State on questions like jurisdiction is, I think, impossible in any real sense. My clerical opponent maintains that the Church holds a precise, defined position within the State. I maintain, on the contrary, that the Church ought to include the whole State and not merely occupy a corner of it. And if that is for some reason impossible at present, then it ought to be set up as the direct and chief aim of the future development of Christian society!”
“Perfectly true,” Father Païssy, the silent and learned monk, agreed with fervor and firmness.
“The purest Ultramontanism!” cried Miüsov impatiently, crossing and recrossing his legs.

“Oh, well, we have no mountains,” cried Father Iosif, and turning to the elder he continued: “Notice the answer he gives to the following ‘fundamental and essential’ propositions of his opponent, who is, you must remember, a churchman. First, that ‘no social organization can or ought to claim for itself the power to dispose of the civic and political rights of its members.’ Secondly, that ‘criminal and civil jurisdiction ought not to belong to the Church, and is inconsistent with its nature, both as a divine institution and as an organization of men for religious purposes.’ And finally, thirdly, that ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’”

“What an unworthy play on words for a churchman!” Father Païssy could not keep from breaking in again. “I have read the book you answered,” he added, turning to Ivan, “and I was astounded by the words ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’ If it is not of this world, then it cannot exist on earth at all. In the Gospel, the words ‘not of this world’ are not used in that sense. Playing with such words is indefensible. Our Lord Jesus Christ came to set up the Church on earth. The Kingdom of Heaven, of course, is not of this world but in Heaven. But it is entered only through the Church, which has been founded and established on earth. And so a frivolous play on words in this connection is unpardonable and improper. The Church is, in truth, a kingdom, ordained to rule, and in the end it must undoubtedly become the kingdom ruling over all the earth. For that we have the divine promise.”
He stopped speaking suddenly, as if checking himself. After listening attentively and respectfully, Ivan went on, addressing the elder with perfect composure and the same ready cordiality as before:

“The whole point of my article is that during the first three centuries Christianity existed on earth only in the Church and was nothing but the Church. When the pagan Roman Empire wanted to become Christian, it inevitably happened that, in becoming Christian, it took in the Church but remained a pagan State in very many of its departments. In reality this was bound to happen. But Rome as a State kept too much of pagan civilization and culture—for example, in the very aims and fundamental principles of the State. The Christian Church, entering into the State, could of course give up no part of its fundamental principles—the rock on which it stands—and could pursue no aims other than those ordained and revealed by God Himself. Among them was that of drawing the whole world, and therefore the ancient pagan State itself, into the Church. In that way (that is, looking to the future), it is not the Church that should seek a definite position in the State, like ‘every social organization,’ or as ‘an organization of men for religious purposes’ (as my opponent calls the Church). On the contrary, every earthly State should in the end be completely transformed into the Church and become nothing but a Church, rejecting every purpose out of keeping with the aims of the Church. None of this will degrade it in any way, or take from its honor and glory as a great State, or from the glory of its rulers. It only turns it from a false, still pagan and mistaken path onto the true and rightful path, which alone leads to the eternal goal. That is why the author of the book _On the Foundations of Church Jurisdiction_ would have judged correctly if, in seeking and laying down those foundations, he had regarded them as a temporary compromise, unavoidable in our sinful and imperfect days. But as soon as the author ventures to declare that the foundations he now proposes, some of which Father Iosif just listed, are permanent, essential and eternal, he goes directly against the Church and its sacred and eternal vocation. That is the gist of my article.”

“That is, in short,” Father Païssy began again, stressing each word, “according to certain theories only too clearly formulated in the nineteenth century, the Church ought to be transformed into the State, as if this were an advance from a lower form to a higher, so that she would disappear into it and make way for science, for the spirit of the age, and for civilization. And if the Church resists and is unwilling, some corner will be set aside for her in the State, and even that under control—and this will be so everywhere in all modern European countries. But Russian hopes and conceptions demand not that the Church should pass into the State as from a lower type to a higher, but, on the contrary, that the State should end by becoming worthy to be only the Church and nothing else. So be it! So be it!”

“Well, I must say you’ve reassured me somewhat,” Miüsov said with a smile, crossing his legs again. “So as I understand it, the realization of such an ideal is infinitely remote, at the second coming of Christ. That’s up to you. It’s a beautiful Utopian dream of the abolition of war, diplomacy, banks, and so on—something like socialism, in fact. But I imagined it was all meant seriously, and that the Church might be going to try criminals _now_, and sentence them to beatings, prison, and even death.”

“But if there were nothing but the ecclesiastical court, the Church would not sentence a criminal to prison or to death even now. Crime and the way it is viewed would inevitably change—not all at once, of course, but fairly soon,” Ivan replied calmly, without flinching.
“Are you serious?” Miüsov gave him a sharp look.

“If everything became the Church, the Church would exclude all the criminal and disobedient, and would not cut off their heads,” Ivan went on. “I ask you, what would become of the excluded man? He would then be cut off not only from men, as now, but from Christ. By his crime he would have sinned not only against men but against the Church of Christ. Strictly speaking, this is so even now, but it is not clearly stated, and very, very often the criminal of today comes to terms with his conscience: ‘I steal,’ he says, ‘but I don’t go against the Church. I’m not an enemy of Christ.’ That is what the criminal of today keeps telling himself. But when the Church takes the place of the State, it will be hard for him, standing against the Church all over the world, to say: ‘All men are mistaken, all in error, all mankind is the false Church. I, a thief and murderer, am the only true Christian Church.’ It will be very hard to say this to himself. It takes a rare combination of unusual circumstances. Now consider the other side, the Church’s own view of crime. Is it not bound to give up its present, almost pagan attitude? Is it not bound to change from the mechanical cutting off of its tainted member to protect society, as now, into wholly and honestly adopting the idea of the regeneration of the man, of his reformation and salvation?”
